title: Egyptian Macarona Béchamel with Spiced Beef & Golden Top
dek: A sliceable Egyptian pasta bake layered with penne, warmly spiced beef and a thick, silky béchamel, with reliable make-ahead and doneness cues.
image_alt: Square slice of Egyptian macarona béchamel showing penne, a spiced minced-beef center and a thick browned white-sauce top, with the casserole behind
ingredients: 1 tablespoon fine sea salt, for the pasta water
1 tablespoon neutral oil, plus more for the baking dish
1 medium yellow onion, finely diced (about 1 1/2 cups)
1/2 cup (45 g) finely grated Romano or Parmesan cheese

instructions.name: Heat the oven and prepare the pan
instructions.text: Set a rack in the middle of the oven and heat to 375°F (190°C). Lightly oil a 9-by-13-inch metal or glass baking dish. Set the eggs on the counter so they are not refrigerator-cold when they meet the warm béchamel.

instructions.name: Undercook the penne
instructions.text: Bring 4 quarts of water to a boil and add 1 tablespoon salt. Cook the penne for 2 minutes less than the package's al dente time; it should bend but still have a firm core. Reserve 1 cup pasta water, drain well and do not rinse. Spread the pasta on a rimmed sheet pan so carryover heat does not soften it.

instructions.name: Brown the beef thoroughly
instructions.text: Heat 1 tablespoon neutral oil in a 12-inch skillet over medium-high. Add the beef in a single layer and leave it undisturbed for 2 minutes. Break it into small crumbles and cook for 4 to 5 minutes more, until no pink remains and the largest pieces reach 160°F on an instant-read thermometer. Transfer the beef to a bowl, leaving about 1 tablespoon fat in the skillet.

instructions.name: Concentrate the spiced meat layer
instructions.text: Reduce the heat to medium. Add the onion and cook for 5 minutes, stirring, until translucent and lightly golden. Add the garlic, tomato paste, allspice, cinnamon and paprika; stir for 1 minute. Return the beef, then add the crushed tomatoes, 3/4 teaspoon salt, black pepper and 1/3 cup water. Simmer for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until thick enough that a spoon drawn through the skillet leaves a trail. Remove from the heat.

instructions.name: Build a pale roux
instructions.text: Melt the butter in a heavy 4-quart saucepan over medium heat. Whisk in the flour and cook for 2 minutes, whisking constantly. The paste should bubble and smell lightly nutty but stay pale; browning it deeply would mute the clean color of the finished béchamel.

instructions.name: Whisk the béchamel until it coats a spoon
instructions.text: Add the warm milk 1 cup at a time, whisking each addition smooth before adding the next. Stir in 1 teaspoon salt, nutmeg and white pepper. Bring to a gentle simmer, then cook for 5 to 7 minutes, whisking often and scraping the corners, until thick enough to coat the back of a spoon. Remove from the heat and whisk in the Romano. Cool for 5 minutes.

instructions.name: Temper the eggs without scrambling
instructions.text: Whisk the eggs in a medium bowl. Slowly whisk in 1 cup of the warm béchamel, starting with a tablespoon at a time. Pour that mixture back into the saucepan while whisking. The sauce should be thick and smooth; if it forms a few small egg threads, pass it through a fine-mesh sieve before assembling.

instructions.name: Layer for clean, visible slices
instructions.text: Toss the drained penne with 1 1/2 cups béchamel, adding 2 to 4 tablespoons reserved pasta water only if the pasta looks dry. Spread half the pasta firmly and evenly in the dish. Spoon the beef mixture over it without pressing it into the tubes. Add the remaining pasta, pour the remaining béchamel over the entire surface and spread it into the corners. Sprinkle evenly with mozzarella.

instructions.name: Bake to a golden, safe center
instructions.text: Set the dish on a rimmed sheet pan and bake uncovered for 40 to 45 minutes, until the edges bubble, the top is golden in patches and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center reads at least 165°F. If the center is hot but the top is pale, broil 6 inches from the element for 1 to 2 minutes, watching continuously.

instructions.name: Rest before slicing
instructions.text: Rest the casserole uncovered for 15 minutes so the béchamel and pasta set into distinct layers. Cut into 8 squares with a thin knife, wiping it between cuts. Finish with sliced scallions only if using and serve warm.

why_it_works: Undercooking the penne by 2 minutes preserves the tube shape while the pasta absorbs measured moisture from the sauce in the oven.
Reducing the beef mixture until a spoon leaves a trail prevents tomato liquid from bleeding into the white sauce or making the center slide.
A 6-tablespoon butter roux thickens 5 cups of milk enough to hold a generous top layer without becoming pasty after baking.
Tempering the eggs with gradually added sauce creates a sliceable béchamel while keeping the eggs smooth rather than curdled.
Coating the pasta with only part of the béchamel keeps the tubes moist but leaves enough sauce for the defining thick white cap.
A 15-minute rest is structural, not decorative: steam subsides and the starch, egg and dairy matrix firms enough for clean squares.
swaps: Use ground lamb or a half beef, half lamb mixture in place of beef; both should reach 160°F before the tomato mixture is reduced.
Rigatoni or ziti can replace penne. Avoid long noodles or tiny macaroni because they do not build the same stable, visible layers.

For a meatless version, replace the beef with 12 ounces finely chopped cremini mushrooms plus 1 1/2 cups cooked brown lentils. Cook the mushrooms until their liquid evaporates before adding the tomato paste.
Romano gives the sauce a sharper, saltier finish; Parmesan is milder. The mozzarella top is a home-style variation and can be omitted for an all-béchamel surface.
Two percent milk works, but the sauce will be less lush. Do not use unsweetened plant milk unless it is neutral, heat-stable and unflavored; its thickening behavior and taste can differ.
storage: Cool leftovers and refrigerate in shallow covered containers at 40°F or below within 2 hours; eat within 4 days. Reheat covered portions in a 350°F oven with 1 tablespoon milk around the edges for 20 to 25 minutes, or microwave at 70% power in 60-second intervals, until the center reaches 165°F. To freeze, cool completely, wrap individual pieces airtight and freeze for up to 2 months; thaw overnight in the refrigerator before reheating. The béchamel may be slightly less silky after freezing.
notes: Cultural and naming note: Egyptian macarona béchamel is a baked pasta casserole built from tubular pasta, seasoned minced meat and a substantial white-sauce layer. Egyptian food-history writing connects the dish to the Greek pastitsio that entered Egyptian restaurant and home cooking through nineteenth- and early twentieth-century Mediterranean exchange. This version keeps the defining layered structure while labeling mozzarella as an optional home-style finish.

Photo-match record: the CC0 photograph is captioned Egyptian Macarona Béchamel (Pastitsio). It visibly shows a square slice with penne above and below a minced-meat center, a thick pale béchamel cap, browned patches and a casserole dish behind; every defining visible element is named in the title, ingredients, method and alt text.

9-by-13-inch assembly ratio — bottom: half of the béchamel-coated penne pressed into an even 3/4-inch layer; middle: all of the reduced beef mixture spread edge to edge; top: remaining penne plus all remaining béchamel. Keeping the meat away from the sauce pan and reducing it first are the two best defenses against sliding layers.

Doneness checklist — bubbling around the full perimeter; golden patches across the surface; no liquid pooling at the corners; 165°F at the center; 15 minutes of uncovered resting before the first cut. Color alone cannot confirm that the dense center is hot.

Make-ahead plan: assemble through the mozzarella, cool each component before layering, cover and refrigerate for up to 24 hours. Bake directly from the refrigerator at 375°F for 50 to 60 minutes, tenting loosely if the top browns before the center reaches 165°F.

Food-safety note: USDA guidance uses 160°F for ground beef and 165°F for casseroles and leftovers. This recipe checks the beef in the skillet and the assembled casserole separately because the second reading confirms the coldest center has reheated safely.

faqs.q: Why did my macarona béchamel fall apart when I sliced it?
faqs.a: The most common causes are fully cooked pasta, a loose meat sauce, thin béchamel or skipping the rest. Stop the penne 2 minutes before al dente, reduce the beef until a spoon leaves a trail, simmer the béchamel until it coats a spoon and rest the baked casserole for the full 15 minutes. A cold casserole slices even more neatly for make-ahead portions.

faqs.q: Can I assemble Egyptian macarona béchamel the day before?
faqs.a: Yes. Cool the pasta, meat and béchamel until just warm, assemble, cover and refrigerate for up to 24 hours. Bake it cold at 375°F for 50 to 60 minutes rather than 40 to 45, and require 165°F at the center. Do not leave the assembled dish at room temperature while waiting for the oven.

faqs.q: Does Egyptian macarona béchamel have to include cheese?
faqs.a: No. The defining top is béchamel, and many versions rely on egg-enriched white sauce rather than a separate cheese layer. Romano in the sauce and mozzarella on top make this version savory and visibly golden, but you can omit the mozzarella and replace the Romano with 2 additional tablespoons butter for a cheese-free dairy béchamel.
